what_happened.summary: A grounder that rolls down the first base line, goes foul, then rolls back into fair territory is still live. If the first baseman touched it in fair territory before it settled, the umpires treat it as fair, so the out at first stands. Safe and out calls are judgment calls in Little League, so they cannot be protested and the call stays.

output.call_type_rationale: The umpire must first judge where the ball was when touched or where it settled, then the written fair-ball rule decides whether that makes the ball fair and the batter out.

channel.how: Ask calmly between innings or after the game if you want to understand the fair-or-foul call; do not argue with the umpire during the game.

output.teachable_moment: Run every ball you hit until you hear the umpire say Foul or Time, because a ball near the line can come back fair.

individual: Run hard to first on every batted ball until you hear Foul or Time.
Practice running through first base and taking a few steps past the bag before looking for the ball.
team: At practice, roll balls down the first base line that go foul and come back fair so everyone learns the rule.
Have a coach act as umpire and signal fair or call foul while batters and fielders play the ball out.
at_home: With a parent, roll a ball along a line in the yard or driveway and shout fair or foul so you keep running until you hear the call.

missing_facts: fair/foul determination rule for a batted ball that rolls foul then back fair before being touched by a fielder

life_lesson.text: Finish the job even when you think the play is over. Keeping going until the umpire stops you helps on the diamond and in school and life.

lessons.title: Play until you hear 'foul'
lessons.principle: Every batted ball is live until the umpire says otherwise. Players don't decide fair or foul; the umpire does. So run hard and play the ball until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'

lessons.title: Run hard through the finish
lessons.principle: Run every ball out at full speed, through first base and until the play is over. Slowing down at the end costs more outs than speed ever gains.

situations.name: Slow roller rolls foul, then back fair before first base
situations.offense: It's a fair ball, so the batter is a runner and the out at first stands. A ground ball that hasn't reached first or third base isn't foul just because it crossed the line: it's judged where it stops or where a fielder first touches it. This one rolled foul, came back, and was picked up in fair territory, so it was fair and in play. Umpires usually signal a fair ball by pointing toward fair territory without saying anything; only foul is called out loud. Batter: run on every ball you hit until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'
situations.defense: Pick the ball up and make the play: step on first or throw there. A slow roller near the line that's still rolling can be left alone; if it stops or you touch it in foul territory before it reaches the base, it's foul. Fielders, like batters, play until the umpire stops it.
situations.common_mistakes: The batter stands at the plate because the ball crossed the line once; the fielder picks it up and freezes; the umpire's fair signal is late or small, so nobody sees it; coaches on both sides shout directions and the players try to learn the rule in the middle of the play. Fix: the plate umpire points fair clearly the moment the ball is touched in fair territory, and coaches teach 'run until you hear foul' at practice, not during the play.
